entries.topic: Stop distance vs. holding horizon: the √t noise band, and why entry location (not stop width) is the binding lever on multi-week swings
entries.summary: A stop has one job: fire on evidence the thesis broke, not on ordinary noise. Kaminski & Lo (SIFR RR 63, 2008; J. Financial Markets 18(C):234-254, 2014) prove that under a random walk, stop-loss rules ALWAYS decrease expected return; they only add value when returns exhibit momentum/positive serial correlation, generating what they call a 'stopping premium' proportional to return persistence (empirically 50-100bp/month during stop-out periods, US equities 1950-2004). So a stop placed inside the random-walk noise band is a pure expected-return tax. The quantitative half comes from volatility scaling: noise excursion grows with the SQUARE ROOT of time, so a stop sized off a one-day ATR is roughly √N too tight for an N-day hold (√45 ≈ 6.7). Danielsson & Zigrand (J. Banking & Finance 30(10):2701-2713, 2006) show the √t rule is only valid under iid normal returns and under jump diffusion 'leads to a systematic underestimation of risk, whereby the degree of underestimation worsens with the time horizon [and] the jump intensity' — so for equities with earnings inside the horizon, ATR×√N is a FLOOR on the noise band, not a ceiling. The decisive consequence: NO static entry stop inside a 15% cap can cover a 45-day noise band. This is not a reason to widen stops (the cap and the 2:1 RR floor forbid it) — it is the proof that stop width is not the free lever. Entry location is. The stop must only survive until the thesis STARTS working, which is why the Chandelier Exit (verified formula
key_points: Kaminski & Lo: under a random walk stops ALWAYS reduce expected return; they only pay when momentum/serial correlation is present. A stop inside the noise band is a pure tax.
Noise scales with √t: a 1-day ATR-based stop is ~√N too tight for an N-day hold (√45 ≈ 6.7). The min_stop_distance_pct floor is a ONE-DAY band, not a horizon band.
Danielsson & Zigrand: under jumps the √t rule UNDERSTATES risk, and worsens with horizon length — so ATR×√N is a floor on the true band, not a ceiling.
Therefore no static entry stop within the 15% cap can cover a 45-day noise band. Stop width is not the lever; ENTRY LOCATION is.
The stop must cover the noise band of the time until the thesis starts working (≈ATR×√days_to_catalyst), not the full horizon. Near catalyst + entry at support = a survivable stop.
Chandelier anchors to the 22-day HIGH, not entry (22d High − 3×ATR), precisely because a moving anchor re-measures the band as the trade works. Verified formula.
Gap risk means 1R is not a guaranteed loss: SEC says a stop is a trigger, not a fill price. DELL realized -1.43R through a 408 stop. Budget realized risk at ~1.3-1.5R on jump-prone names.
MAE (tighten stops to where winners live) contradicts the above but needs ~100 trades; at 2 closed trades it is unusable — sample-size rules outrank it.
entries.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, run the horizon-vs-noise test: compare my stop distance (%) against the name's daily ATR% × √(days until the nearest real catalyst) — NOT the full holding_horizon_days. entries.topic: Correlation-adjusted position sizing: co-moving names are one bet (the effective-number-of-bets collapse), not many, and why that governs portfolio heat and the theme-risk cap
entries.summary: Diversification by COUNT is an illusion; only diversification by uncorrelated risk FACTORS reduces risk. For N equally-sized positions each with volatility sigma and pairwise correlation rho, portfolio volatility is sigma*sqrt([1+(N-1)*rho]/N): at rho=0 that is sigma/sqrt(N) (full benefit), but at rho->1 it goes to sigma, i.e. the N positions behave as ONE. The clean summary statistic is the effective number of independent bets, N_eff ~= N/[1+(N-1)*rho]; two names at rho~0.85 give N_eff~1.08 -- essentially a single bet. That is exactly my realized loss history: DELL and HPE were two tickers on ONE hyperscaler_server_capex driver, so a Meta-overbuild headline took both out at once, and my '2 positions' were 1 correlated bet the whole time. Attilio Meucci's Effective Number of Bets (exponential Shannon entropy of the diversification distribution) makes the same point formally: hidden correlation makes a book that LOOKS like N holdings act like ~1 exposure to one factor, and PCA can even hide this (minimum-torsion/factor framing is needed to see it). The Turtle system encoded the practitioner version as hard unit caps -- 4 units single market, 6 closely-correlated, 10 loosely, 12 in one direction -- precisely so a cluster of correlated trades could not become one oversized bet. Two cautions from the sources: (1) correlations RISE toward 1 in exactly the tail shock you are stopping for, so a benign-looking rho understates joint downside; (2) correlated stops fire and GAP together
key_points: Portfolio vol for N equal positions = sigma*sqrt([1+(N-1)*rho]/N); as rho->1 the whole book collapses to one position's risk. Two 20%-vol names equal-weight: 14.1% vol at rho=0 vs 20% at rho=1 -- the entire benefit is gone.
Effective number of independent bets N_eff ~= N/[1+(N-1)*rho]; two names at rho~0.85 = ~1.08 bets. DELL+HPE was arithmetically one bet, and it is my only realized-loss cluster.

The diagnostic question (per practitioners): 'what single event would make most of my open positions lose at once?' If positions co-move >~0.7 or share a demand_driver, they are ONE bet regardless of ticker count or GICS label.

Meucci's ENB / diversification ratio: count-based diversification is meaningless; only exposure to uncorrelated factors counts, and hidden correlation can make an apparently-diversified book a concentrated one-factor bet.
Turtle caps (4 single / 6 closely-correlated / 10 loosely / 12 one direction units) are the practitioner encoding of 'do not let correlated trades stack into one oversized bet.'

Tail behavior is worse than the average rho suggests: correlations spike toward 1 in a shock, and correlated stops fire and gap together -- so sizing, not the stop, is the defense against a correlated gap-through (DELL filled ~4.5% past its stop).

Honesty check: a common 'effective risk = risk*sqrt(N*rho)' blog example (6x1% at 0.85 -> 13.6%) is inconsistent -- combined risk cannot exceed the sum of parts; use the portfolio-variance identity instead.

When shared_left_tail is true, actively prefer a low/negative corr_to_book diversifier (diversifier=true) over a higher-conviction clone of what I already own, because at book level the clone adds almost no independent bet. entries.topic: The pullback-continuation entry in a leading uptrend: buying the low-volume ('no-supply') dip to structural support instead of chasing the fresh high
entries.summary: The pullback-continuation setup buys a temporary dip inside an established uptrend rather than chasing a new high. It works because two well-documented return patterns run on different clocks: medium-term momentum persists over roughly 3-12 months while short-term returns (days to a few weeks) mean-revert (the short-term reversal effect, Blitz/Huij, Alpha Architect summaries). Buying the short-term dip in a medium-term leader therefore rides the durable trend while getting a better price and a tighter stop. The whole craft is separating a HEALTHY pullback -- shallow, orderly, on DRYING volume, the Wyckoff/VSA 'no supply' bar where professionals simply stop selling -- from a REVERSAL, which is sharp, wide-range, and comes on HIGH volume that breaks structure ('supply'). Volume is the tell, not price alone. Minervini's version: after a valid advance a healthy pullback retraces modestly (~8-10% max, or back to a rising 50-DMA), volume contracts into the dip and re-expands on the resumption; common support zones are the 20-EMA, 50-DMA, and the 38-62% Fibonacci band. Critically, the entry is the RESUMPTION, not the dip itself -- you wait for volume to dry up and then a confirming up-move, you do not catch the falling knife. This is the one thing my own 12-year ablation confirmed: no_supply_pullback scored +0.22pp (21d) / +0.25pp (63d), the only positive read among ~25 indicators tested, measured on names already above their 200-DMA. key_points: Two clocks: 3-12mo momentum persists while days-to-weeks returns revert (short-term reversal) -- a pullback in a leader rides the trend at a better price and a tighter stop.

Volume is the discriminator: healthy pullback = shallow, orderly, volume DRYING UP (Wyckoff 'no supply'); reversal = sharp, wide-range, HIGH volume breaking support. A high-volume dip is supply -- pass.
Depth/zone guides: after a valid advance ~8-10% max or back to a rising 50-DMA; support at the 20-EMA, 50-DMA, or 38-62% Fibonacci retracement.
Enter the RESUMPTION, not the dip: wait for volume to dry up, then a confirming up-bar / short-term-level reclaim -- never buy the falling knife.
My only ablation-confirmed edge: no_supply_pullback +0.22pp (21d)/+0.25pp (63d) on names above the 200-DMA -- this playbook is the one I have first-party evidence for.
Reconciles my own bundle: high-ADX breakouts measured -0.35pp (fail) but the low-volume pullback measured positive -- in an extended trend, buy the orderly dip, don't chase the breakout.
Win rates: distrust the '82%' SEO claim; credible ~55-65% for MA-reversion pullbacks, weaker in low-turnover names and stretched momentum-gap conditions -- real edge, not universal.
Buying at support satisfies KB-2388376284: the same stop then sits beyond the sqrt-t noise band, so entry location -- not stop width -- carries the risk.
entries.how_to_apply: When a universe leader (above a rising 50/200-DMA, positive rel_strength_1m and 3m vs SPY) pulls back, treat it as a BUY candidate only when the dip is orderly AND volume_signal reads no_supply_pullback -- my one ablation-confirmed tell; a high-volume, wide-range dip is supply, so pass. Do not buy the dip itself: wait for volume to dry up and a resumption bar (reclaim of a short-term level or a pocket-pivot-style up day), which is the concrete fix for my ANET regret_miss where I watched the pullback and never entered. Anchor the stop just below the pullback's swing low or the named anchored_vwap level so the same stop sits beyond the noise band per KB-2388376284, hold the 2:1 RR floor honestly, and let the chandelier trail run the winner rather than tightening early. Prefer pullbacks with a catalyst inside a short window so entry-to-event noise is small, and size the initial entry at 50-70% then scale in only on confirmed strength. In an already-extended, high-ADX leader this low-volume pullback -- not the fresh breakout my own data shows fails at ADX>25 -- is where the fat pitch lives.

entries.topic: Exit on pre-committed invalidators, not real-time conviction: the disposition effect, 'resulting', and why the written plan (not the mood) must license every early exit
entries.summary: My single binding process_fail is HPE: I closed a LOSING position ahead of its stop on a 'conviction crack,' graded process_fail with tag missing_invalidators_on_plan. The behavioral literature explains why that class of decision loses systematically. Odean's canonical study of 10,000 brokerage accounts (Journal of Finance 53:1775-1798, 1998) documents the disposition effect: investors are 1.5-2x more likely to sell a winner than a loser, and crucially this is NOT justified by subsequent returns - the losers they clung to did not go on to outperform, so the discretionary exit judgment was simply wrong on average. The practitioner consensus fix is pre-commitment: a 1991 study found the disposition effect weakens sharply when people sell at predetermined rules/intervals instead of discretionarily, and the reliable antidotes are predefined exit rules set BEFORE entry, mechanical stop/target execution, and documenting the rationale so the exit is a rule-check rather than a fresh emotional decision. Annie Duke's 'resulting' sharpens this: judging a decision by its outcome corrupts learning, so you must write the reasoning and the expected outcome distribution up front and grade the exit against THAT, not against the P&L - which is exactly why DELL (stop fired as planned, still a loss) is a process_win while HPE (discretionary, happened to save a few dollars) is a process_fail. key_points: Odean 1998 (JoF 53:1775-1798): the disposition effect is real and NOT vindicated by later returns - discretionary 'when to exit' judgment loses on average, so it must be replaced by rules.
Pre-commitment is the measured fix: the disposition effect weakens when exits fire on predetermined rules; predefined criteria + mechanical execution + written rationale beat real-time discretion.

Duke's 'resulting': grade the exit against the plan you wrote at entry, never against the P&L - a planned stop-loss is a process_win (DELL), a discretionary exit is a process_fail even if it saved money (HPE).
My HPE loss wasn't classic disposition effect (I cut a loser early) but the same root: emotion overrode a plan that had no written invalidators to test the exit against.
Action bias and omission bias are the same disease, sign-flipped: over-trading AND the 6-day unwind paralysis both come from letting an emotional state, not the written bar, decide.
The antidote to cutting winners early is mechanical: sell_fraction partials at >=2R plus the chandelier trail, so the rule (not the itch to lock in) manages the runner.
Silence-of-invalidators is a HOLD signal: if no written invalidator fired, 'conviction cracked' or 'the tape feels bad' is not a licensed reason to exit before stop/target/horizon.

Grade every exit against the entry plan, not the P&L (Duke's resulting): a stop firing as written is a process_win even at a loss, a discretionary save is a process_fail. entries.topic: Estimate-revision momentum: how upward EPS/revenue revision breadth leads price via the post-forecast-revision drift, and why breadth + price-confirmation beats a lone divergence
entries.summary: Analyst estimate revisions are a genuine, well-documented fundamental predictor: prices underreact to revisions and DRIFT in their direction for roughly six months (the post-forecast-revision drift, PFRD). Old evidence (Givoly/Lakonishok-era) put the up-minus-down revision portfolio spread near ~3% annually, and later work finds aggregated revisions can predict post-earnings-announcement returns as well as or better than the earnings surprise itself. The mechanism is the reason it persists and is the key to trading it: the DIRECTION of revisions is far more persistent than the direction of returns because analysts themselves underreact — anchoring-and-adjustment and herding make them revise incrementally and insufficiently, so a first up-revision statistically predicts more up-revisions (Chen et al. 2020, JBFA). Signal quality is not uniform. A single revision is mostly noise, and noise/bias in analyst forecasts rises with the forecast horizon (Noise in Expectations, RFS 2024), so BREADTH — how many analysts are raising vs cutting over ~100 days — and NEAR-TERM (next-quarter/next-FY) revisions carry the real signal, not one far-out number. Consistency matters more than magnitude: high-innovation revisions that are CONSISTENT with the prior trend and with price action drive more drift than larger 'reversal' revisions that fight the tape (Chen 2025), and revisions that merely drift toward existing consensus ('low-innovation') carry little information. key_points: PFRD is real and persistent: prices drift in the revision's direction for ~6 months; my 3-90d swing only needs to capture the front of a durable trend, which is favorable.
The tradeable core: revision DIRECTION is more persistent than return direction because analysts underreact/anchor/herd — a first up-revision predicts more up-revisions.
Use BREADTH (raisers minus cutters over ~100d), not a single estimate change; a lone revision is noise.
Prefer NEAR-TERM revisions (next-Q/next-FY); noise and bias grow with forecast horizon.
Consistency > magnitude: revisions that agree with the prior trend and price drive more drift than larger reversal revisions; revisions merely converging to consensus carry little info.
Highest-conviction setup = up-revision breadth CONFIRMED by constructive price (this is exactly my post_earnings_drift_candidate gap_held_revisions_up flag).

The revisions-up / price-weak divergence (MU) is the seductive trap: sometimes underreaction opportunity, sometimes price-knows-first; resolve by diagnosing why price is weak and waiting for price confirmation, not by buying estimates alone.
But do not reflexively SKIP the divergence either — that is my documented over-skip; watchlist it with a price-reclaim trigger and act when price confirms.
entries.how_to_apply: Treat fundamental_screen.top_upward_revisions and revision_direction=up / positive eps_growth_next_yr_pct as a real candidate lane, not background noise — this is the direct fix for repeatedly defaulting MU-type names to the watchlist and eating +15% regret_misses. When underwriting one, weight BREADTH of near-term (30-day EPS / next-Q) revisions over any single number, and require the revision trend to be consistent (up-revisions following up-revisions), because that persistence is where the edge lives. For the fat pitch, demand price CONFIRMATION of the fundamentals — positive rel_strength_1m/3m, no_supply_pullback or a reclaim — which is precisely the post_earnings_drift_candidate gap_held_revisions_up read; that revisions-and-price-AGREE case gets full weight and can clear the bar now. For the pure divergence (revisions up, price down, MU-style), do NOT buy estimates into a falling knife and do NOT reflexively skip: name in the thesis whether price weakness is temporary (cyclical/sector/tax/macro) or structural (ai_at_risk, cycle-peak earnings embedding the cycle continuing), put it on the watchlist with a specific price-reclaim trigger, and promote to BUY when price confirms —

entries.topic: The options-implied expected move and earnings IV crush: reading options_signals to time swing entries around binary prints, and why the implied move is a market-priced noise band
entries.summary: Options price a stock's expected move as Price × IV × √(DTE/365) ≈ one standard deviation; a fast earnings shortcut is ~0.85 × the ATM front-month straddle (tastytrade uses a weighted straddle+strangle version). Empirically the stock stays inside that ±1σ band ~68-70% of the time, so the implied move is a genuine, horizon-scaled noise band — not a forecast of direction. Crucially it is priced too WIDE on average: implied vol exceeds realized vol by roughly 3-5 percentage points annualized (the volatility risk premium), and a CBOE study of ~10 years of S&P 500 earnings found the actual post-print move was SMALLER than the straddle-implied move in ~72% of cases. But the distribution has fat tails — the ~30% of moves that break the band include the outliers that gap through any stop (the SMCI ~20% preliminary-print pop is exactly this tail). Before a known binary event, front-month IV inflates and the term structure goes into BACKWARDATION (near-term IV > far-term); the moment the event resolves, IV crushes 30-50% (40-55% on high-IV names like NVDA/TSLA) within hours and the term structure normalizes. For a directional trader, holding a swing stop THROUGH a print means betting on a coin-flip gap you are not paid to take: the pre-print premium is a cost to option holders, but to an equity holder the print is just an un-stoppable jump on top of the normal diffusion. The cleaner trade is around it — enter 1-2 days after the print once the gap settles, IV has crushed, and the direct
key_points: Expected move = Price × IV × √(DTE/365) ≈ 1σ ≈ 0.85 × ATM straddle; stock stays inside it ~68-70% of the time — it's a horizon-scaled NOISE band, never a direction call.

The band is priced wide: IV > RV by ~3-5pp/yr (volatility risk premium); a CBOE 10-yr study found the real earnings move was smaller than implied ~72% of the time. But fat tails mean the ~30% of breaks contain the account-denting gaps.

Term-structure backwardation (front IV > back IV) + elevated iv_rank = an event premium is priced into the front month; this is the detector that a binary is coming even without a clean calendar date.
IV crush: front-month IV peaks the session before the print and drops 30-50% (40-55% on high-IV names) within hours; the term structure then normalizes.

A single-day earnings expected move is a DISCRETE jump layered on top of the diffusion noise band — no valid swing stop inside the 15% cap survives it, so the honest move is to trade AROUND the print, not through it.
Post-print entry (1-2 days later) lets the gap settle and IV crush, giving a fairer price with the binary removed — the same window where post_earnings_drift / gap_held_revisions_up pays.
Chasing the gap on the print bar is buying the fat-tail move with no clean stop; the disciplined re-entry is the light-volume retest (per KB-6241168493), not the climax bar.
entries.how_to_apply: Before any BUY, read options_signals.expected_move_pct and term_structure together with days_to_earnings: if a print (or a backwardation + high-iv_rank event premium) falls inside holding_horizon_days, default to trading AROUND it — either enter after the print once IV crushes and the gap settles, or shorten the horizon so the stop never has to survive the binary, because the earnings expected move is a discrete jump no ATR-floored stop inside the 15% cap can cover (this refines KB-2388376284: the implied move is a market-priced noise band, superior to ATR×√N, and stop_engineering already floors the stop at ½ the expected move — treat that as a one-day floor, not horizon-adequate through an event). Only hold through a print when the binary itself is the thesis (a stated drift/gap_held_revisions_up setup per KB-2596574918), and then size on gap-adjusted risk. entries.topic: Reading the consolidation base to define a precise, auditable pivot trigger — and why the throwback to the level, not the breakout through it, is the higher-expectancy swing entry
entries.summary: The base-and-pivot framework (O'Neil's cup-with-handle, Minervini's VCP) exists to convert a fuzzy 'wait for confirmation' into ONE auditable price level: the pivot — the base's prior peak / handle high, the last ceiling of overhead supply. A valid VCP base shows 2-3 successive contractions where BOTH price range AND volume tighten, each smaller than the last, signaling sellers drying up; the classic entry then buys as price clears the pivot on volume ~40-50% above average. entries.topic: The catalyst-in-a-downtrend setup: why good news on a below-MA / near-52-week-low name has the WEAKEST expected drift, and the confirmation-gated re-entry that separates a real turn from a dead-cat bo
entries.summary: My biggest single cluster of shadow-book regret_misses is the same setup every time — a positive catalyst (beat-and-raise, raised guidance, insider cluster) on a name trading BELOW its 50/200-DMA, which I reject for 'lack of confirmation' and then never re-enter when confirmation arrives (CLS +10.5%, NOW +12%, IBM +11%, NOC, HCA, SMCI). The naive read is 'I was too cautious.' The evidence says the opposite about the SKIP and pinpoints my real error elsewhere. George, Hwang & Li (Anchoring, the 52-Week High and PEAD) find post-earnings drift is concentrated by nearness to the 52-week high: investors anchor on the high and underreact to GOOD news when a stock is NEAR its high (strong upward drift, the tradeable long), but that underreaction — and therefore the drift edge — is WEAKEST when the same good news lands on a name far from its high / near its low; the drift only re-ignites once the 52-week high (or the relevant overhead level) is reclaimed and 'the market wakes up.' So the best PEAD longs are good-news LEADERS, not good-news names in a downtrend. Bulkowski's dead-cat-bounce database says the same from the price side: large event declines (almost all company-specific bad-or-good-then-faded news) typically bounce ~50% of the drop on FADING volume, make a lower high, then resume the decline 'at a more leisurely rate.' Practitioner consensus (bear-market-rally and reversal writing, O'Neil's follow-through logic) converges on the tell: a dead-cat bounce fails at resistance
key_points: Academic core (George/Hwang/Li): good-news drift is STRONGEST near the 52-week high and WEAKEST near the low — so a catalyst on a below-MA/near-52w-low name is the low-edge PEAD cell, not a hidden gift; the edge re-ignites only when overhead resistance is reclaimed.

Bulkowski dead-cat-bounce data: big event declines usually bounce ~half on fading volume, form a lower high, then keep declining — chasing the first pop in a downtrend is statistically the wrong side.

Dead-cat-bounce vs real reversal, the checklist: FADE = lower high + shrinking volume + breaks prior low; TURN = higher-high-and-higher-low, successful retest of the low on LOWER volume, rising volume on advances, reclaim/hold above the declining 50-DMA.

O'Neil follow-through logic applied to a single name: don't try to catch the bottom; require a confirmation up-day that shows institutional accumulation (a reclaim held for 2-3 sessions on volume) before committing.

My real error was NOT the skip — it was rejecting-and-forgetting: no armed re-entry trigger, so when the turn confirmed I wasn't watching. The fix is a specific structural trigger on the watchlist, not a same-day chase.
This fills a genuine gap: KB-6241168493 (pullback-continuation) only covers names already ABOVE the 200-DMA; it says nothing about a name coming off a bottom, which is where these regrets live.

entries.topic: Market breadth as the regime aggression dial: participation, the divergence/thrust asymmetry, and why breadth is a CONDITION not a timing signal
entries.summary: Breadth measures how many stocks are PARTICIPATING, which no index level can reveal - an index at new highs on narrowing participation and one on broadening participation look identical in SPY but are different regimes. The classic bearish read is a breadth DIVERGENCE: the index prints a new high while the advance-decline line makes a lower high and the share of stocks above their 200-DMA falls, meaning the advance is being carried by fewer, larger names. Documented cases precede 1987, 2000, 2007 and 2021 tops (the NYSE A-D line peaked nearly two years before the 2000 Nasdaq crash). BUT the honest empirical record on top-CALLING is weak: a divergence is a condition, not a timing signal - it can persist for weeks, months, or over a year, produces frequent false positives during ordinary corrections, and tops are inherently hard to time. Practitioner consensus is to treat divergence as a yellow flag and wait for a PRICE trigger (a 50-DMA or trendline break) before acting. The important asymmetry: bullish breadth THRUSTS off washout lows (Zweig-type surge from <40% to >61.5% of stocks advancing within ~10 days) are far more reliable than bearish divergences - they are rare (~18 since 1945) but historically preceded ~23% average 12-month S&P gains with a near-perfect record, because bottoms follow repeatable patterns and the market drifts up over time (fewer false positives than tops). entries.topic: Pyramiding into a winner: adding above blended cost while the trailed stop keeps total risk flat, and why the chandelier trail is what funds the second unit
entries.summary: My KB covers scaling OUT (KB-6231300499) but not scaling IN, though CLAUDE.md makes adds a core mechanic (max 2, above blended cost, never average down, and 'stops trailed above cost free their budget'). Pyramiding = adding to a position the market has confirmed, building the largest size at the base with smaller adds up the trend; it is the exact opposite of averaging down (adding to a loser hoping it recovers). The unifying risk rule across every source is one sentence: a new unit's risk may ONLY be funded by unrealized profit the earlier units have already banked, expressed as a trailed stop that has ratcheted up enough that combined risk-to-the-shared-stop stays at or below where it started. The Turtles operationalized this: add one unit every 0.5N (half an ATR) in your favor, cap at 4 units per market, and move the whole position's 2N stop up so it sits 2N below the most recent add — so as you pyramid, aggregate risk stays bounded and eventually goes to breakeven-or-better on the combined book (secondary summaries of the Original Turtle Rules; I could not fetch the primary PDF/theturtletrader page — socket errors — so I flag the Turtle specifics as reported-by-secondary). Two schools disagree on add SIZE and I keep the disagreement honest: the Turtles use EQUAL units and rely on the moving stop to cap risk, while most practitioners (TradersPost, heygotrade, QuantStrategy) insist each add be SMALLER than the last (e.g. 1.0 / 0.5 / 0.25) so the blended entry stays close to
key_points: Pyramiding adds to WINNERS on confirmation; averaging down adds to LOSERS — the validator already enforces the distinction (adds only above blended cost, never below).

The only safe funding source for a new unit's risk is profit the earlier units have locked in via a trailed stop that has moved up; no trail lift = the add is just fresh full risk stacked on the book.
Turtle rule set (reported by secondary summaries): add every 0.5N in favor, max 4 units, move the shared 2N stop up to 2N below the latest entry; each unit sized so ~1N ≈ 1% of account.
Run ONE unified stop for the whole pyramid (the chandelier trail), never a separate stop per layer.
Never invert the pyramid — later adds bigger than the base spike blended cost and let a V-shaped reversal turn a confirmed winner into a loss (most-cited failure mode).

Practitioner consensus favors DECREASING add sizes so the blended entry stays near the first entry; Turtles used equal units + a rising stop. Both cap risk; the decreasing version also protects the RR-to-target.
Pyramiding is expectancy-positive because it concentrates capital into the few confirmed big winners that carry trend edge — 'it's how you manage the position, not the win rate.'

entries.topic: Anchored VWAP as an auditable reaction level, not a directional signal: where to anchor (event/swing-high/swing-low), the trapped-buyer cost-basis mechanism, and using it for stop/target/entry geometr
entries.summary: Anchored VWAP (AVWAP, pioneered by Brian Shannon) is the volume-weighted average price since a CHOSEN event rather than since the session open, so it reads as the average cost basis of everyone who transacted from that anchor onward. The entire craft is anchor SELECTION: the good anchors are genuinely meaningful events — the earnings-gap candle, a major-volume/breakout day, a significant swing high, a significant swing low, an IPO or major-news bar — which is exactly what my bundle's anchored_vwap.anchor_reason already encodes deterministically (breakout_above_20d_high, else the highest-volume session). The reason a well-anchored line acts as support/resistance is participant psychology plus institutional benchmarking: when price sits below a post-earnings AVWAP the late buyers are underwater and become persistent overhead supply that sells into rallies to get back to flat, and when price returns to the AVWAP those same buyers reach breakeven — so the level is where the largest cohort's cost basis concentrates. The mechanism is self-reinforcing because institutions verifiably benchmark executions to VWAP (Biais, Glosten & Spatt 2005; VWAP is shown to be the optimal execution strategy for a risk-neutral trader in the volume-augmented Almgren-Chriss model, arxiv 1408.6118 — both reported via secondary summaries, I could not fetch the primaries due to socket errors). Crucially, every serious source agrees AVWAP is NOT predictive of DIRECTION — 'it describes where value was estab
key_points: AVWAP = average cost basis since a chosen event; the anchor IS the edge — anchor to earnings-gap candles, major-volume/breakout days, and significant swing highs/lows, not arbitrary dates.

It works via trapped-buyer psychology + verifiable institutional VWAP benchmarking: below a post-event AVWAP = underwater buyers = overhead supply; a reclaim/hold = breakeven relief and a change of character.

NOT a directional signal — literature ('describes value, not future price') and my own 12-year ablation (above -0.12pp / below +0.06pp) agree. Never cite 'above AVWAP = constructive' or reject a setup for being below it.

What survives is GEOMETRY: use the AVWAP as an auditable reaction level for entries (retest/hold of a rising swing-low AVWAP), stops (below the reversal candle low or a decisive close below the AVWAP), and targets (just below a declining swing-high AVWAP = overhead supply).
VWAP pinch = converging swing-high and swing-low AVWAPs = compression/decision zone; between two AVWAPs is 'no man's land' where the edge dissolves.
Confluence multiplies reliability: an event AVWAP stacking with a prior high and the daily/weekly VWAP is a much stronger level than any single line.
Limitations to respect: subjective anchor selection, unreliable on low-volume/illiquid names, whipsaws when flat, and thin public backtest evidence (30-trade samples).

On an episodic-pivot / earnings-gap name (KB-3704904010), anchor mentally to the gap candle: price below that AVWAP means trapped buyers overhead, and a reclaim-and-hold is the change-of-character to promote on; use the gap-day low or the AVWAP as the structural stop reference that clears the ATR/expected-move floor. entries.summary: The two sizing questions - how much to risk PER trade, and how much ACROSS correlated trades - are one theory. (1) The Kelly criterion f* = W - (1-W)/R maximizes long-run geometric growth and outputs the fraction of capital to RISK, mapping exactly onto the 1%-of-equity, entry-to-stop budget. On realistic swing parameters (2:1 RR so R~2, 40-55% win rates) full Kelly is 10-32.5%, so 1% is ~1/10 to 1/30 of full Kelly - deeper than quarter-Kelly, and that is CORRECT, not timid. Three reasons the literature is unanimous on: parameter uncertainty (MacLean-Thorp-Ziemba: a 10% edge overestimate causes ~50% overbetting at full Kelly, and with ~2 closed trades my true edge is essentially unknown, so Kelly says bet near zero); the growth curve is a downward parabola g~(2c-c^2)*g_max where half-Kelly keeps ~75% of growth at half size, growth hits ZERO at 2x Kelly and goes negative beyond - so the over side has a cliff the under side does not, making underbetting strictly the safer error; and Thorp always ran fractional Kelly in practice. (2) But Kelly assumes INDEPENDENT bets; correlated simultaneous positions share ONE Kelly budget (multivariate f* = Sigma^-1 (mu-r)). Diversification by COUNT is an illusion: for N equal positions at pairwise rho, vol = sigma*sqrt([1+(N-1)*rho]/N), collapsing to sigma as rho->1, and the effective number of independent bets N_eff ~= N/[1+(N-1)*rho] - two names at rho~0.85 is ~1.08 bets. entries.topic: Stop slippage and overnight/event gap risk: why realized R systematically undershoots the underwritten 2:1, and how to build a gap buffer into sizing, setup selection, and stop width
entries.summary: A regular stop-loss is a market order the instant it triggers: the broker guarantees a FILL, never a PRICE, so through a gap or a fast move it executes at the first available print, not at your level (Schwab, Optimus Futures, Topstep). The 1R I underwrite is therefore a FLOOR on the loss, not a ceiling, and realized R can and does exceed it. My own two closed trades prove it: DELL's 408 stop filled at 389.75, 4.47% and 0.55 ATR through, turning a planned -1R into realized -1.43R (r_gap 3.17), and across both closes mean realized R was -0.985 against a claimed mean RR of 1.765 - the 2:1 that cleared the validator gate did not survive contact. Two frictions with very different magnitudes are at work: intraday slippage on liquid large-caps is small (~0.1%, and momentum/breakout entries slip somewhat worse because you buy what is already moving), but overnight and event GAPS are the fat left tail - SPY gaps >2% on ~18 days a year and single names far more, with earnings the single largest controllable driver (financial-spread-betting, tradingsetupsreview, enlightenedstocktrading; the frequency and magnitude figures are reported by secondary practitioner sources, not primary data I could verify). Expectancy is W*avgWin - L*avgLoss measured in R, so when avgLoss drifts beyond -1R via slippage and gaps the edge erodes directly, and below roughly +0.2R of expectancy costs and slippage consume most of what is left (systemr.ai, traderssecondbrain, quantstart); tail losses greater than
key_points: A regular stop becomes a MARKET order once triggered: fill guaranteed, price not. It cannot cover a gap - it fills at the first available print, so the 1R I underwrite is the floor on a loss, not the ceiling.

My record confirms the erosion: DELL filled 0.55 ATR / 4.47% through its 408 stop (-1.43R vs planned -1R); both closes averaged -0.985R realized against 1.765 claimed RR. Claimed 2:1 did not survive contact.
Gaps >> intraday slippage in magnitude. Liquid large-cap slippage is ~0.1%; the real damage is the overnight/event tail, and scheduled earnings are the #1 controllable gap trigger.
Slippage and gaps erode expectancy directly by pushing avgLoss past -1R; below ~+0.2R expectancy, costs eat most of the edge, and >1R tail losses hurt geometric growth asymmetrically (KB-2999578881).

Widening the structural stop lowers slippage-as-a-fraction-of-R: a 0.55-ATR gap-through is +55% of a 1-ATR stop but only +27% of a 2-ATR stop - an independent reason to aim wider than the bare ATR floor.
Momentum/breakout entries and thin names slip worst; chasing extension compounds gap exposure, so prefer liquid names and buy at structure, not extended.
Guaranteed stops (fee-based, fill at level through gaps) are CFD/spread-bet only - unavailable here. Manage gap risk by sizing, setup selection, and avoidance, not by any order type.
entries.how_to_apply: Underwrite every BUY on realized-R, not planned-R: treat the 2:1 that clears the validator as the optimistic case, and on any name with event or gap exposure demand a genuine cushion (aim ~2.5:1+) rather than scraping 2.0, because a single 0.5-ATR gap-through converts a 1R plan into ~1.4-1.5R realized, exactly as DELL did. Respect the earnings/binary rule as a GAP rule and not just an IV-crush rule (extending KB-8308262054): never carry an ATR-floored stop through a print inside holding_horizon_days since no stop inside the 15% cap can cover the jump - trade around it by entering after the gap settles, or size for gap-adjusted risk with an explicit earnings_case, and always honor the 3-day blackout. entries.topic: Valuation is a weak timing tool over a swing horizon: why a high forward multiple on a quality/momentum leader is not a standalone skip reason, and what 'expensive' actually flags (embedded expectatio
entries.summary: My single most expensive recurring shadow-book mistake is rejecting high-quality momentum leaders for being 'too expensive' or 'extended' and then watching them run +10%: NET twice (+10.3%/+10.4%, cited 'P/E 231, 984% premium'), SNOW (+10.9%, '146x forward'), S (+11.6%, '+30% is extension'). The literature says valuation's predictive power is both HORIZON- and LEVEL-dependent, and neither dimension supports using a multiple to time a 3-90 day single-stock swing. Asness/AQR is the honest counterweight: high AGGREGATE Shiller P/E does lower forward INDEX returns and worsen tail outcomes, but only over 7-10+ year windows and with enormous variance even over decades - it is a planning input, not a timing signal, and it is about the index, not a single stock over weeks. Momentum makes this concrete - high-momentum stocks are almost definitionally low-value/expensive (one secondary source puts the overlap near 96%, flagged reported-by-secondary), value and momentum are negatively correlated yet both pay (AQR 'Value and Momentum Everywhere'), so rejecting a leader FOR being expensive is rejecting the momentum edge itself. key_points: Valuation predicts returns only at the INDEX level over 7-10+ years (Asness), with huge variance - it has essentially no power to time a single stock over a 3-90 day swing.

Return = yield + earnings growth +/- multiple change; over swing horizons the multiple CHANGE dominates and is driven by expectations revisions/flows, not reversion of the starting level (Bogle/Robeco/Blitz).
Momentum by construction buys expensive stocks and still pays; value and momentum are negatively correlated (AQR VME). Skipping a leader for a high multiple discards the momentum edge.

A high multiple = high EMBEDDED expectations (Rappaport/Mauboussin). The stock moves on actual-minus-expected, so 'priced for perfection' names are punished on strong-but-short prints - the risk is at the binary, not in the level.
A premium to sector median or a high forward P/E is DESCRIPTIVE color, not a variant_perception and not a standalone skip reason - identical logic to the dead-indicator veto rule.
The genuine swing risk from a rich multiple is asymmetric gap-down into earnings; the fix is the earnings blackout / trade-around-the-print, not staying out of the name entirely.
Mirror of the existing cyclical-value-trap rule: don't buy a low multiple blindly (cycle-peak), and don't reject a high multiple blindly (expectations, not overpricing).

entries.topic: Maximum Adverse/Favorable Excursion as a path diagnostic: winner-MAE is the empirical stop check, live heat is read from position_stop_cushion, and two closed trades cannot refit a stop
entries.summary: John Sweeney (TASC Oct 1985 / Jan 1991; Campaign Trading, Wiley 1996; Maximum Adverse Excursion, Wiley 1997) defined MAE as the worst unrealized loss from entry to the lowest subsequent low on a long, and MFE (MaxFE) as the peak unrealized gain, independent of the final P&L. His rule, quoted from the MAE book, is that good trades generally do not go far against you while bad ones do: if the entry rules can distinguish winners from losers, their MAE distributions separate, and the cliff where a trade becomes more likely to end badly than profitably is where the stop belongs. Van Tharp (Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom, 1998) restates the same observation — 'Good trades seldom go too far against us' — and lists winner-MAE as one legitimate way to set a stop, alongside a noise-beyond stop of roughly 2.7–3.4× the 10-day ATR (about 3 ATR; he suggests even wider, ~10 ATR, for long-term stock holdings). Practitioner write-ups (LuxAlgo; JournalPlus; Traders Second Brain) operationalize this as a scatter of MAE vs final P&L in R or ATR units, plus an MFE capture rate (realized gain / MFE) as the exit-quality diagnostic. Sources disagree on the action: some secondary blogs say if winner-MAE sits at 0.3R against a 1R stop you should tighten to 0.5–0.6R; JournalPlus says if 30%+ of winners cluster just beyond the stop you should widen; Tharp himself warns the MAE stop is after-the-fact and easy to curve-fit, and that the wider ~3 ATR stop is generally more profitable than a tight one
key_points: Sweeney's rule: if the entry has edge, winner-MAE and loser-MAE separate; the stop belongs just beyond the winner cluster, not at a round number or a support line everyone else uses.
MAE/MFE measure the PATH, not the blotter: two +$200 winners can be a near-stop rescue and a 50%-captured runner; final P&L hides both stop quality and exit leakage.
Normalize in R or ATR, never raw dollars, and require 30–100 trades per setup before changing a stop. Two closed trades are anecdotes. Tharp flags curve-fitting; LuxAlgo flags regime shift.

Do not take the blog 'tighten to winner-MAE' half as a standing rule. Tharp's 3×ATR class of stop and this system's 1.5–2×ATR swing floor plus gap buffer are the prior; MAE may later justify WIDENING if winners cluster inside the noise band, not tightening into gaps.

MFE capture (realized / peak open profit) grades exits. Retail sources put typical capture near 35–55% and call 65–80% healthy for swings — those bands are practitioner-illustrative, not a measured law. A break-even move once MFE hits +0.5R or +1R is a common MAE-blog tactic and is the opposite of this system's coded trail (the chandelier never jumps to breakeven at +1R). For 3–90 day swings that early BE move guts expectancy.

Live MAE is already in the bundle: position_stop_cushion.cushion_in_atr. Under ~1 ATR (inside_noise_band) means ordinary noise can finish the 1R. Stalled (14d, ±3% of cost) is low MAE and low MFE together — opportunity cost, not a stop-width problem.

entries.topic: The pre-print fork: run-up and exit before the print vs hold-through vs wait, when earnings sits 4-30 days out
entries.summary: A scheduled earnings date 4-30 days away is not one decision and is not a skip. It is a three-way fork between (1) a shortened-horizon run-up that is flat before the print, (2) a deliberate hold-through of the binary, and (3) waiting for the post-print reaction. These rest on different evidence. Frazzini and Lamont (NBER w13090, 2007) document an earnings-announcement premium: stocks rise around scheduled prints, a long announcers / short non-announcers book earned over 60 bp per month, the effect is strong in large caps, lasts about 20 days / four weeks, and shows up in samples back to 1927; they tie it to predictable volume and attention-driven buying. Barber, De George, Lehavy and Trueman (Journal of Financial Economics 2013) replicate the premium globally (~60 bp/month long-short; ~76 bp in the US book) but disagree on the mechanism: the bulk of the premium is realized BEFORE the announcement day, pre-announcement returns arrive with REDUCED volume (the opposite of an attention-buying surge), and idiosyncratic volatility spikes in the three days centered on the print — they read it as compensation for uncertainty about the information to be released. Savor and Wilson (Journal of Finance 2016) give a third account (systematic risk): firms scheduled to report earned about 9.9% annualized abnormal return. I cannot adjudicate the mechanism from this session; what the three papers share, and what I will use, is the TIMING: average excess return accrues on the way INTO a known
key_points: A print outside the 3-day coded blackout is a fork, not a veto: run-up (flat before the print), hold-through (binary is the thesis), or wait (post-print playbook).

The academic announcement premium (Frazzini-Lamont; Barber et al.; Savor-Wilson) accrues INTO the scheduled date — Barber's event study is positive on days -10 to 0, with the vol spike on days 0 and +1 — so the harvestable swing is the approach, not the jump.
Sources disagree on WHY (attention/volume vs pre-print uncertainty premium vs systematic risk). They agree on WHEN. Use the timing; do not pick a mechanism as a thesis pillar.
The run-up is a tailwind of a few percent, not a 10% setup. Take it only when an existing structure already has honest 10% and 2:1 to a level that can print BEFORE the blackout.

Hold-through is a different trade from the run-up: it needs an explicit earnings_case, gap-adjusted R (aim ~2.5:1+), and a real cushion versus the options expected move — otherwise flatten before T-3.

PEAD / gap-and-hold is the third fork (already in KB-3704904010 / KB-2596574918), not a reason to sit out a live pre-print setup. Classic large-cap SUE drift has faded; do not wait for a 60-day SUE residual that the literature says is mostly gone in liquid names.
A new BUY whose horizon still contains the print is a hold-through whether you admit it or not. If you will not write earnings_case, the horizon and the target must both expire before the 3-day gate.
entries.how_to_apply: When a universe name has a live structure (no_supply_pullback, throwback to a written pivot, or a day-after-gap pullback) and earnings_week / days_to_earnings puts the print 4-30 days out, do not reject it for the print — that is the LITE miss (+12.1% after 'earnings in 4 days'). Fork it. Run-up (default when 2:1 and 10% clear to a named pre-print level): enter on the existing trigger, set holding_horizon_days so the plan expires at least one session before the 3-day blackout, put target_price just below the first overhead supply that can be reached in that shortened window (prior high, discounted measured move, or the swing-high anchored VWAP), and plan the SELL_TO_CLOSE before T-3. If that geometry cannot clear 10% and 2:1 without inventing a post-print target, the run-up is a pass — do not inflate the target and do not silently turn it into a hold-through. Hold-through only when the binary itself is the thesis: write earnings_case, size for gap-adjusted R using options_signals.expected_move_pct (if the implied move is larger than stop distance the stop is theater), and require a real cushion (trail already lifting, or unrealized room that can absorb the expected move) per Minerv

entries.topic: 1-month vs 3-month relative strength vs SPY: 3m filters leaders, 1m times the pullback, and they mean opposite things when they diverge
entries.summary: The two RS fields on every scanned row are not interchangeable leadership scores. Jegadeesh and Titman (Journal of Finance 1993; NBER w7159, 1999) document that stocks with high returns over the prior 3–12 months continue to outperform over the next 3–12 months (~1% per month long-short in the original sample; the 1990s out-of-sample window paid about the same). Their construction, and the standard Carhart/AQR follow-ons, SKIP the most recent month because of the short-term reversal Jegadeesh (Journal of Finance 1990) found: prior-month winners underperform the next month (~2% per month in 1934–1987). Da, Qian and Gao (NY Fed Staff Report 513, 2011) later show that this 1-month reversal is weaker in large, analyst-covered names (standard reversal three-factor alpha 0.33%/month, t=1.37, insignificant) and is mostly a WITHIN-industry, non-fundamental residual — liquidity shocks on recent losers, sentiment on recent winners — so I should not treat a high 1m RS on a liquid large-cap as a fade, nor a low 1m RS as a buy-the-washed-out-laggard signal. Practitioners (O'Neil CAN SLIM; Minervini Trend Template) still want high RS — Deepvue, summarizing O'Neil's 500-winner study 1953–1985, reports an average RS Rating of 87 BEFORE the major advance; Minervini's template (via Finer Market Points) wants RS >70, ideally 90+ — but they are using a 12-month PERCENTILE rank, often reverse-engineered as 40% on 3-month return and 20% each on 6/9/12 (Worden/AmiBroker reconstructions; not an offi
key_points: 3–12 month relative performance is the documented momentum edge (Jegadeesh-Titman); academic portfolios skip the last month on purpose so 1-month reversal does not contaminate the ranking.
rel_strength_3m_pct vs SPY is the leadership FILTER: positive = in the winner cohort; negative = a laggard, even if it just popped on news.

rel_strength_1m_pct is the EXTENSION CLOCK, not a second leadership score. Strongly positive 1m on already-positive 3m = extended; modestly negative/flat 1m with still-positive 3m = a leader pulling back.

1-month reversal is a long-short, often-illiquid effect and is weak in large analyst-covered names (Da/Qian/Gao). Do not fade a liquid large-cap winner on 1m RS, and do not buy a washed-out laggard because 1m RS is negative.
Our RS is excess vs SPY, not IBD's 1–99 percentile. Do not mentally translate '+X% vs SPY' into 'RS 90.' momentum_6m_pct (raw) plus 3m RS vs SPY is closer to the 6-month JT formation than 1m RS is.
rel_strength_vs_sector failed its 12-year ablation (same score as an arbitrary grouping). It is descriptive colour for where a name sits in its group, not evidence of leadership.
Daniel-Moskowitz: momentum crashes after declines + high vol, in the rebound. In unwind/hostile tapes, 3m-RS leadership is the left tail, not the fat pitch.
Novy-Marx (intermediate 7–12m) vs IBD (overweight 3m) is a real disagreement. For this swing book, treat 6m/3m as who, 1m as when — and do not rank 'higher 1m RS = better idea.'
entries.how_to_apply: On every candidate, read rel_strength_3m_pct (and, when present, momentum_6m_pct) BEFORE 1m RS. A pullback-continuation or throwback (KB-6241168493 / KB-9692173165) is only a leadership buy when 3m RS vs SPY is still positive: that is a JT winner resetting, which is the 'leader that held up' O'Neil/Minervini are pointing at. If 1m RS is also strongly positive, the name is extended — do not chase the spike (the RBRK pattern); write would_buy_at as the no_supply_pullback or throwback to the pivot and wait. If 1m RS has gone modestly negative or flat while 3m RS remains positive, that DIVERGENCE is the constructive pullback, not a broken leader — do not reject it for '1m RS rolled over.' If 3m RS is negative, a 1m pop is a laggard bounce: route it through the confirmation-gated re-entry of KB-2665689010, do not promote it as leadership. Never cite rel_strength_vs_sector_* as a reason to buy or skip, and never rank ideas by who has the hottest 1m RS. When momentum_health is unwind or the tape has just washed out, do not add more 3m-RS leadership (Daniel-Moskowitz crash window); take the code's 0.5x haircut as given and prefer catalyst/value/diversifier setups instead of more of the sam

entries.topic: R-multiple expectancy and losing-streak math: why a 2:1 book is profitable at 40% wins, why three losses cannot license a stand-down, and why clustered same-theme losses are one bet not a broken proce
entries.summary: Van Tharp's R-multiple (Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom, 1993/2007) normalizes every close as outcome divided by initial entry-to-stop risk, so a +2R winner and a −1R stop are comparable across names and sizes. Expectancy is then E = (W × avg_win_R) − ((1−W) × avg_loss_R). At this system's 2:1 floor and a 40% win rate with avg_loss = 1R, E = +0.20R per trade (0.40×2 − 0.60×1); breakeven win rate is 1/(1+2) = 33.3%, so 40–55% is the profitable band CLAUDE.md already names, not a hope. Sources disagree on the swing RATIO: ForTraders (2026) wants 1:3+ on multi-day holds because overnight/gap costs eat planned R, while the 2:1 math is already positive if avg_loss stays near 1R — I keep the validator floor and treat the overnight cost as a realized-R haircut (KB-9689938621's ~2.5:1 cushion on gap/event names), not as a higher coded bar. The same formula shows why cutting winners early is fatal: if avg_win collapses toward 1R while losses stay 1R, 40% wins go to E ≈ 0. The sequence of three closed trades (DELL −1.43R with 0.55 ATR gap-through; two HPE exits at −0.54R; mean realized R −0.837 vs mean claimed RR 2.15) is not a measured expectancy. Tversky and Kahneman (Psychological Bulletin, 1971) document the law of small numbers — people treat a tiny sample as representative of the generating process; with 0 wins in 3 trials the 95% upper bound on true win rate is roughly 63% (rule of three), so n=3 cannot distinguish a 40% system from a coin flip. Consecutive-loss math makes t
key_points: Expectancy E = (W × avg_win_R) − ((1−W) × avg_loss_R) is the number that decides whether the game is worth playing; win rate alone is a vanity metric.
At 2:1 with avg_loss = 1R, breakeven W is 33.3% and 40% wins produce +0.20R/trade; that is the mathematical reason the validator's 2:1 floor exists.
Realized avg_loss above 1R (DELL −1.43R) can flip a 40%/2:1 book to negative E; that is a gap/slippage problem, not a reason to raise the 2:1 floor or to skip the next clean setup.

n=3 with 0 wins cannot estimate W or E (law of small numbers); Tharp wants 30–100 R-outcomes before SQN/expectancy is more than noise, and this system's anecdote/caution/binding gates already encode that.

A 3-loss streak is a ~22% event at the design 40% win rate and the expected longest streak in 100 independent trades is ~9; abandoning a positive-E process because the first three lost is the error the math names.
When the three losses share a demand_driver they are one correlated bet, so they diagnose theme stacking (2% theme / factor_map) rather than 'swing trading does not work.'
Risk is controlled by SIZE (1% budget, 0.5% probe, 0.5× unwind haircut, 8% heat). Standing down double-counts the same caution and produces zero calibration data.
entries.how_to_apply: After any losing streak — including the 2026-08-19 HPE probe that closed −0.54R on resting_stop_breached — judge the next candidate on its own thesis, geometry, and validator floors (2:1, 10% upside, stop outside stop_engineering.min_stop_distance_pct, 3-day earnings blackout only). Grade the book in realized R (track_record / exit_execution_grades.realized_r), not win rate: if avg_loss is drifting above 1R, demand the ~2.5:1 cushion and liquid/non-event entries of KB-9689938621 on the NEXT buy rather than standing down; if the losses cluster on one demand_driver, the next BUY should prefer a different driver or a diversifier (portfolio_risk.diversifier / low corr_to_book) and must respect the 2% theme and factor-stack caps — that is rotation of the bet, not abstention. entries.topic: Undercut-and-rally (Wyckoff spring): the confirmation entry is the reclaim of undercut support, never the undercut bar, and a failed reclaim is a real breakdown
entries.summary: An undercut-and-rally is one event with three names: Wyckoff's spring (price briefly breaks a trading-range low then closes back inside the range), the swing-trader U&R (TraderLion lists it as an entry tactic; Qullamaggie calls the same bar a demand-tail shakeout of the 10/21-EMA or prior low), and the microstructure stop-run (Bookmap, ITI). The mechanism is not mysticism. Osler (NY Fed SR 150 / JIMF 2005) shows stop-loss orders cluster at obvious levels and, when triggered, produce a burst of positive-feedback flow; her FX results are statistically significant at the hourly horizon and not at the daily, so I transfer the clustering fact, not the cascade magnitudes, to this EOD equity book. Once that liquidity is consumed the market either rejects (no acceptance below, reclaim and hold of the old range) or accepts (prior support becomes resistance and the breakdown continues). ITI is the honest fork I will use: a sweep is an information event, not a buy signal, and the third bucket is no-trade when reclaim/acceptance is unclear or invalidation is too wide. Practitioner sources agree on the entry I can actually execute: do not buy the undercut wick. TradingSim and Wyckoff Analytics want the close back above support, preferably on expanding volume, with the stop just below the spring low; Villahermosa splits springs by depth (shallow/low-volume can be bought on the reclaim, deep/high-volume springs need a successful higher-low test on reduced volume) and I keep that split as de
key_points: U&R / spring / stop-run are the same sequence: obvious support is undercut, resting stops fire, then price either reclaims the range (rejection) or accepts below it (real breakdown).
A sweep is not a BUY. Classify first: reversal (reclaim and hold), continuation (acceptance below), or no-trade (ambiguous or stop too wide to clear 2:1 / the 15% cap).

Never buy the undercut / selling-climax bar. Entry is the daily close back above the named level; if the undercut was deep or climactic, wait for the higher-low test on lighter volume (this system's no_supply_pullback language) before adding or promoting.

entries.topic: ADX/DMI as a lagging description of how extended a trend already is: ADX>25 is a late-entry warning, ADX<20 cannot veto a live thesis, and direction lives in +DI vs -DI
entries.summary: J. Welles Wilder introduced the Average Directional Index in New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978) as a measure of trend STRENGTH, not direction: ADX is the smoothed absolute gap between +DI and -DI divided by their sum, so a violent downtrend prints a high ADX the same way a violent uptrend does. Direction is a separate read — +DI above -DI is up-pressure, the reverse is down-pressure. Wilder’s commodity-daily rule of thumb (StockCharts ChartSchool; Investopedia, Cory Mitchell CMT) is ADX>25 = a trend is present, ADX<20 = no trend, with a gray zone between; his original system bought the +DI/-DI cross only when ADX was already above 25. That construction is late by design: ChartSchool notes the nested Wilder smoothing takes on the order of 150 periods to stabilize, and Wikipedia is explicit that ADX is lagging — a trend must already exist before the line says so. Serious practitioners disagree with using the LEVEL as a gate. Charles LeBeau (TradingMarkets, 15 Apr 2008; with David Lucas, Computer Analysis of the Futures Market, 1992), who also invented the chandelier exit this system already runs, wrote that Wilder ‘got our basic understanding off to a bad start’ by emphasizing level: an ADX of 20 rising steeply is more predictive of trendiness than an ADX of 40 that is flat or declining, and a one-bar rise of 0.25+ is the significance threshold he used. John Murphy’s Law #9 (StockCharts, 5 Dec 2025) takes the same slope view and, crucially, wants ADX used to choos
key_points: ADX measures how one-sided the recent ranges have been, not which way or whether a thesis is valid; +DI vs −DI carries direction, ADX does not.

Wilder’s >25 / <20 thresholds were built for commodity daily charts and are late by construction because of heavy smoothing; ChartSchool itself warns the ADX filter ‘tends to filter as many good signals as bad.’

LeBeau and Murphy: slope beats level. A rising ADX from a low print is the developing-trend read; a high, flat, or falling ADX is the already-extended or exhausting read. This bundle’s compact line does not give slope.

Chesler and this book’s 12-year study agree against the retail rule: ADX contracted below ~20 is when bases resolve, not when breakouts should be distrusted. ADX>25 breakouts were the worst, most stable cell in the study (−0.35pp, 10 of 12 years negative).
Do not conflate ADX<20 with a downtrend. ADX low = neither side dominating (a coil). ADX high and −DI > +DI = a strong downtrend, which is a skip-or-gate-the-long, not ‘chop.’

ADX is a description of how extended the trend already is. It cannot be evidence for a BUY, cannot be the sole ground to reject one, and must not be written into would_buy_at (the sanitizer will strip it; dead_indicator_veto fires if it is the whole argument).
LeBeau, the ADX specialist, said he did not find ADX useful after entry because it is too slow for exits. This system already has his other tool for that job: the 3×ATR chandelier trail.

entries.summary: A time stop exits because the clock ran out, not because price proved the thesis wrong. Van Tharp (Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom, ch. 10) defines it as getting out after a fixed period if you have not made a (sufficient) profit, and he restricts it to short-term trading: do not use one if you are a longer-horizon trader and cannot get back in should the expected move then print. Momentum-burst practitioners sit at the tight pole — Qullamaggie (Jan 2021) sells 1/3–1/2 after 3–5 days, moves the stub to breakeven, and trails the rest on the 10-/20-day — which is a time-based partial plus an early-breakeven rule this system has already refused (the chandelier never jumps to breakeven at +1R, because that guts trend expectancy). Original Turtle trend-following sits at the other pole: exit on a 2N ATR stop or a 10-/20-day channel, not a calendar, so a weeks-long grind can still become the one large R-multiple. Curtis Faith (Way of the Turtle, 2007; the 80-trading-day hold vs Donchian-exit comparison is reported by a secondary summary I could not verify in the primary, so I take only the qualitative claim) later tested a long fixed hold in place of a reactive channel exit and argued the calendar max-hold beat noisy price exits in choppier post-1980s data — that is a MAXIMUM-HOLD time stop, the opposite of a 5-day dump. key_points: Price stop = the thesis is wrong; time stop = the thesis is not working on the schedule you underwrote. They are different tools and both belong on the plan.
A 5–10 day mechanical dump belongs to burst traders. It conflicts with a 3–90 day horizon, the 3×ATR chandelier, and the coded refusal to jump the stop to breakeven at +1R.
Moskowitz–Ooi–Pedersen TSMOM persistence is 1–12 months. Fourteen flat days is not evidence a continuation thesis has failed; it is evidence the capital is idle.
stalled:true (14+ days, within ±3% of cost) is a forced decision — name the remaining wait and its date, or rotate — never 'nothing has changed' and never an automatic SELL_TO_CLOSE.

Do not time-stop a working winner (cushion healthy, invalidators clean, trail lifting). Bank sell_fraction only at ≥2R and let the chandelier trail the rest.

entries.topic: Stop underwriting: the sqrt(t) noise band plus gap-fill slippage make 1R a floor not a ceiling, and entry location — not stop width — is the binding lever
entries.summary: A stop is a trigger that becomes a market order, so 1R is a floor on the loss, not a ceiling (Schwab; SEC). entries.summary: The 50-day and 200-day simple moving averages do two jobs that traders constantly mix up, and only one of those jobs survives contact with the evidence. The first job is a mechanical crossover SYSTEM: buy when the short average crosses the long one (the golden cross), sell on the death cross. Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron (Journal of Finance, 1992) found that variable-length moving-average rules on the Dow Jones Industrial Average, 1897–1986 (25,806 daily observations), produced buy-signal average daily returns of 0.042% versus −0.025% on sells, with lower volatility on the buy side (0.89% vs 1.34% daily standard deviation), and they rejected random-walk, AR(1), GARCH-M and EGARCH nulls. That in-sample gap did not travel. Sullivan, Timmermann and White (Journal of Finance, 1999) rebuilt the tournament those 26 rules were drawn from (~7,846 MA, filter, breakout and OBV variants), applied White’s Reality Check, and found the in-sample champion still looked genuine after the snooping correction — then went dead in the years after 1986. Ready (Financial Management, 2002) argues the BLL profits after costs are a data-snooping artifact. entries.summary: Classic event studies found real announcement reactions and some post-revision drift. Womack (Journal of Finance 1996) reports an unadjusted three-day return of +3.3% on added-to-buy recommendations and -4.3% on added-to-sell, with post-event drift that is modest and short-lived on the long side (+2.4% over one month) but larger and longer on sells (-9.1%, lasting up to six months). Barber, Lehavy, McNichols and Trueman (Journal of Finance 2001; primary PDF read this session) take the investor's calendar-time view: a daily-rebalanced, same-day-close consensus book earned +4.13% / -4.91% annual abnormal gross on the most/least-favored portfolios (Zacks 1986–1996), but a one-week delay dropped the long side to about 2% and a month's delay below 1%, neither reliably above zero; among the few hundred largest firms there was no reliable spread; after transaction costs (turnover sometimes exceeding 400% a year) net returns were not reliably positive. That is the binding result for this EOD large-cap book: we see an upgrade after the gap and we cannot daily-rebalance, so the long-side announcement premium is already gone by the time a proposal can print. Jegadeesh, Kim, Krische and Lee (Journal of Finance 2004) split LEVEL from CHANGE: sell-side analysts systematically recommend glamour (positive momentum, high growth, expensive), the consensus LEVEL only helps among names that already have favorable quantitative characteristics, and among unfavorable-quant names a higher consensus
key_points: Womack: the announcement reaction is real (+3.3% / -4.3% three-day), but leftover UPGRADE drift is modest and ~1 month; SELL drift is larger and longer — this long-only book is on the weaker side of that asymmetry.

Barber et al. 2001 (primary): daily same-day-close consensus alpha is +4.13% gross on the most-favored names and dies under a one-week delay, among large firms, and after costs. An EOD swing book that sees the upgrade after the gap is already in the delay cell.

Jegadeesh et al. 2004: use the CHANGE in consensus, never the LEVEL. Analysts recommend glamour; a crowded strong-buy on an expensive momentum name is the cell where higher ratings predict worse subsequent returns.

Brav-Lehavy: the average 12-month target is 28% above spot. Never set target_price to analyst_ratings.target_mean_price; a PT raise that merely chases a rally is a lagging restatement of price, not a 3-90 day expected return.

Piggybacking is real but not the whole story (Altınkılıç-Hansen vs Li-Ramesh-Shen-Wu). Fork it: if the rec lands on earnings/guidance/8-K, trade THAT playbook and treat the rec as color; if it is standalone, demand Loh-Stulz influence (star, away-from-consensus, paired with an estimate revision) and

Loh-Stulz: only ~12% of rec changes are influential at the stock; more than a third of reactions have the wrong sign. A faded upgrade gap that closes back through the pre-rec close is the tell that this one was in the 88%.

HPE 2026-08-19 is the worked example: a Morgan Stanley upgrade gap bought after it printed, on a large-cap glamour/theme name, with the mean target used as destination. Literature predicted weak remaining edge; giving back the pre-upgrade close was the right invalidator.
entries.how_to_apply: When news_and_catalysts or analyst_ratings shows a rating upgrade or a price-target raise, do not promote to BUY on the rec itself and do not write target_price from target_mean_price or target_vs_price_pct — Brav-Lehavy's 28% average premium is optimism, and CLAUDE.md already forbids citing a Street target as our own. First ask whether the rec piggybacks a dated fundamental: if earnings_week, a retained earnings gap, or todays_8ks/item 1.01 sits under it, route the name through the episodic-pivot or estimate-revision playbook (KB-3704904010 / KB-2596574918) and treat the rec as color, not a second catalyst. If it is standalone, require the Loh-Stulz influence screen (away from consensus, paired with a near-term estimate revision, preferably a star/leader house) AND a held gap (retained_pct not faded); then wait for the day-after first pullback or a no_supply_pullback of the upgrade bar rather than buying the announcement print, place stop_loss below the pre-upgrade close or the gap-day low (at least stop_engineering.min_stop_distance_pct), and confirm 2:1 to the first overhead supply — not to the new PT. entries.topic: RSI-14 as swing-entry timing context: the 40-50 reset in a Stage-2 uptrend is the usable read, RSI>70 is not a sell, and RSI<30 is not a bounce buy
entries.summary: J. Welles Wilder introduced the 14-period Relative Strength Index in New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (1978) as a 0-100 momentum oscillator of Wilder-smoothed up-closes versus down-closes; it is not relative strength versus SPY. His original commodity-daily reading treated RSI above 70 as overbought (a reversal warning) and below 30 as oversold, with divergences and failure swings as the tells — that cartoon is still the one most people quote, and it is the one that fails in equity trends. John Murphy (StockCharts 10 Laws, Law 7) is explicit that oscillators work best in a trading range; StockCharts ChartSchool's McDonald's example shows three successive RSI>70 prints that were consolidations, not tops, because a strong uptrend can stay overbought. Andrew Cardwell and Constance Brown (Technical Analysis for the Trading Professional, as taught on ChartSchool) and Fidelity's RSI guide relocate the range: in an uptrend RSI typically lives in roughly 40-90 with the 40-50 zone acting as support; in a downtrend it lives in roughly 10-60 with 50-60 as resistance (Cardwell's close variant is 40-80 / 20-60). Academic tests of RSI as a standalone RULE are mixed and not robust across markets. Chong, Ng and Liew (MPRA 54149, 2014; daily OECD indices 1976-2002, 10-day holds) found the classic RSI(14, 30/70) mean-reversion rule — buy the reclaim of 30, sell the failure of 70 — produced negative pair-returns in three of five markets, including a statistically significant loss of 1.
key_points: RSI-14 is a speedometer of recent closing momentum, not a valuation, a buy/sell switch, or relative strength vs SPY.

Wilder's 70/30 mean-reversion reading is a range tool. In a Stage-2 equity uptrend, RSI>70 is strength and the 40-50 zone is pullback support (Cardwell/Brown/Fidelity); Murphy is explicit that oscillators work best in a trading range.

Chong, Ng and Liew (2014): the classic RSI(14, 30/70) rule lost in three of five OECD markets (DAX 'sell overbought' -1.049%); the centerline-50 crossover was the better construction and still was not robust across markets.
This book's 12-year study: RSI 40-50 vs RSI>70 is the right sign and too small to trade (0.09pp); RSI<30 inside a 200-DMA uptrend is the only interesting cell and is underpowered (n=257).
Do not skip a 3m-RS leader because rsi_14 is 75, and do not SELL_TO_CLOSE a live winner because it is — that is the RBRK-shaped 'extended' veto in oscillator costume.
Do not buy rsi_14 <30 under the 200-DMA as a bounce; that is a downtrend describing itself, not a mean-reversion gift.

Never write would_buy_at as an RSI cross, divergence, or failure swing — those confirmation legs get stripped. Use RSI only as timing color on a price, structure, catalyst, or no_supply_pullback trigger.
Connors RSI(2) (no stops, 5-day SMA exit) is a different system; do not import it into this 2:1 / ATR-floor / chandelier book.
entries.how_to_apply: On every candidate, read rsi_14 only after above_200dma, trend_up_50_over_200, and rel_strength_3m_pct. If that stack is Stage-2 and 3m RS is still positive, treat rsi_14 in the 40-50 band as the timing description of the no_supply_pullback / 50-DMA tag already in KB-6241168493 / KB-4252672139: write would_buy_at on the named rail or no_supply_pullback, promote on that hold, place stop_loss below the tagged low AND stop_engineering.min_stop_distance_pct, and confirm 2:1 to the first overhead supply — do not promote because RSI printed 45. If rsi_14 is already >70 on a 3m-RS leader, that is strength, not a skip and not a SELL_TO_CLOSE: park the name for the first reset toward 40-50 at the 21-day or 50-DMA, and do not take sell_fraction just because RSI is extended (the first partial still waits for >=2R per KB-6231300499). If rsi_14 is <30 while above_200dma is still true, do not buy that bar — it is the underpowered watch cell; route it through a daily reclaim of the undercut rail (KB-2770353193) or a light-volume retest of the 200-DMA last rail. If above_200dma is false, rsi_14 <30 is not a bounce buy: it is the confirmation-gated downtrend of KB-2665689010. Never write would_buy_

entries.topic: Drawdown recovery math for a 1% risk / 8% heat swing book: recovery is asymmetric, the heat cap is a max-DD budget not a halt, and cash is the zero-drift regime where expected MDD grows as sqrt(T)
entries.summary: A peak-to-trough loss of fraction L requires a gain of L/(1-L) on the remaining capital to get back to the high-water mark — an identity, not a trading theory. The curve is gentle to about 20% (10% needs +11.1%, 20% needs +25%) and then steep (50% needs +100%, 75% needs +300%). Sequential 1% losses compound slightly worse than addition: five losers leave −4.90%, ten leave −9.56%, and it takes 69 consecutive 1% losses to reach −50%. Van Tharp (Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom) uses the same recovery table and then shows that size, not the setup, is the drawdown lever: in his worked sequence of one system, a 2% R produced a 26% max DD, 5% R a 65% DD, and 10% R blew the account. Magdon-Ismail, Atiya, Pratap and Abu-Mostafa (Journal of Applied Probability 2004) give the structural result that expected maximum drawdown of a Brownian motion scales as log T under positive drift, as σ√(πT/2) under zero drift, and linearly under negative drift — a profitable book still draws down, but cash (zero drift) has expected underwater depth that grows with the square root of calendar time. Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin (IJTAF 2005) formalize what an active manager actually feels as risk: Conditional Drawdown, the mean of the worst tail of the underwater curve, with MaxDD and Average DD as limits; our 8% portfolio-heat cap is a crude MaxDD constraint on simultaneous stop-out, not a participation rule. Sequence matters as much as size: Atamus (citing Magdon-Ismail) shows the same multiset
key_points: Recovery is L/(1−L) on remaining capital: 10%→+11.1%, 20%→+25%, 50%→+100%. The job of risk limits is to stay on the flat part of that curve.
At 1% risk, five sequential losers are −4.90% and ten are −9.56%; 69 consecutive 1% losses reach −50%. A 2% paper-book hole is noise on that scale, not a crisis.
Tharp: the same system at 2% / 5% / 10% R produced 26% / 65% / blown in his worked sequence. Size is the drawdown lever; the 1% budget and 8% heat cap are that lever, already set.

Magdon-Ismail et al. (JAP 2004): expected MDD ~ log T with positive drift, σ√(πT/2) with zero drift, linear with negative drift. Standing down (cash, μ=0) is the regime where expected underwater depth grows with sqrt of waiting.

Chekhlov et al. (IJTAF 2005): an active book's risk is the underwater curve (CDD / MaxDD), not variance. The 8% heat cap is a MaxDD budget on simultaneous stop-out — if every stop fires, recovery needed is ~8.7% plus any gap-through, still on the gentle part of L/(1−L).
Drawdown is a path functional: clustered same-theme losses (DELL+HPE, shared_left_tail) are one drawdown event, not two independent 1R hits. That is why the 2% theme / factor-stack caps exist.

Do not martingale to get even. Do not add a blog-style 0.5% de-risk halt on a 2% hole on top of 1%-of-current-equity and the code's unwind 0.5x — that is the stand-down that left the learning loops dark. Percent-of-current-equity is already the brake.
entries.how_to_apply: After every close, compute realized drawdown versus the book's high-water mark and the recovery needed as L/(1−L). If that figure is inside the 8% heat budget — today's four-trade hole is ~2.05% and needs ~2.1%, i.e. one honest 2R winner at the 1% risk budget — judge the next BUY on thesis, geometry, 2:1, the ATR/expected-move stop floor, and the 3-day earnings blackout, not on 'we are in a hole.' Never size up to get even; keep size = (current equity × 1%) / stop_distance_pct so dollar risk auto-brakes as equity falls, which is Tharp's percent-risk model and already how the validator sizes. Never invent an extra de-risk halt or a cash stand-down on top of that 1% and the code's momentum-unwind 0.5x: Magdon-Ismail says cash is the zero-drift cell where expected MDD grows as sqrt(T), and a 2% hole that needs one 2R winner is exactly the setup this paper book's completed-cycle objective is supposed to take. When the losses cluster on one demand_driver or shared_left_tail is true, treat them as one path-DD event: the next BUY should prefer a different driver or a portfolio_risk.diversifier / low corr_to_book name, and must respect the 2% theme and factor-stack caps — that is rotation
