entries.topic: The bull flag after a thrust: buy the tight no-supply flag, not the pole and not the flag-breakout chase
entries.summary: A bull flag is a short continuation, not a multi-week base: a steep several-day pole on heavy volume, then a 3–15 session parallel channel that slopes against the uptrend while volume dries, then a resumption. Edwards & Magee and Murphy call it a half-mast rest in a straight-line move; StockCharts wants the pole to have already broken a level; Investopedia adds that the flag should not retrace past the midpoint of the pole and typically lasts 5–20 bars. Duration is the first honest disagreement: Bulkowski treats anything longer than three weeks as a rectangle or channel, Murphy’s pennants ‘usually last no longer than three weeks,’ while ChartSchool allows one to twelve weeks and calls eight weeks ‘pushing it.’ For this 3–90 day book I keep Bulkowski’s short definition — past ~3 weeks the name is a base (KB-9692173165) or a 50-DMA tag (KB-6241168493), not a flag. The second disagreement is the numbers. SEO posts quote 66–85% win rates and 14% in three weeks; Bulkowski’s own 8/27/2020 update, measured on the short swing rather than the ultimate high, is a 44% break-even failure, a 9% average rise, and only 46% of flags meeting the full measured-move target (pennants are worse: 54% failure, 7% average, 35% meeting target, and the half-staff equality holds only ~30% of the time). Tight flags (little white space, contained in the channel, volume down 74% of the time) beat loose/jagged ones; flags that tilt with the trend underperform flags that tilt against it. The textbook entry
key_points: A flag is a 3–15 day parallel channel after a steep pole; longer than ~3 weeks is a rectangle/base, not a flag. Pennants (converging) are the weaker twin (Bulkowski 54% 5%-failure, 7% average) — do not promote them as a separate setup.

SEO 66–85% win-rate claims are not Bulkowski. His 2020 short-swing numbers are 44% break-even failure, 9% average rise, 46% meeting the full pole projection. Discount the measured move; do not write target_price as pole-height added to the breakout.
Textbook entry is the flag-breakout close. This book’s measured confirmed_breakout cell is negative; no_supply_pullback is the surviving tell. Buy the flag, not the pole and not the breakout chase.

Quality filter: inbound 3m RS still positive (Stage 2), pole unusually steep (not a grind), flag tilts against the trend, tight (contained, little white space), volume declining in the flag, retrace holds above the pole midpoint / roughly <50% of the pole.

Stop sits below the flag low AND stop_engineering.min_stop_distance_pct (aim 1.5–2× ATR). A 4% flag whose ATR floor is 7% is still valid if 2:1 and 10% clear from that wider stop; if they do not, pass — tightness is not a license to hug noise.

High-tight flags (O’Neil: +100% in ≤8 weeks, then 10–25%) are rare and usually untradeable here because a stop under the flag low averaged 26% of price in Bulkowski’s restudy. Only take one if a tighter final contraction lets the stop clear the 15% cap.
entries.how_to_apply: After a steep several-day thrust on a name that still has trend_up_50_over_200 and positive rel_strength_3m_pct — including a held earnings/upgrade gap that is the pole — do not BUY the pole bar and do not reject the leader because rsi_14 printed >70 on that bar. entries.topic: Price gaps as swing geometry: type labels are retrospective, fill folklore is not an edge vs a random walk, and retained_pct plus the pre-gap close are named levels — not a skip or a fade
entries.summary: A daily gap is an untraded range between one session's close and the next open; an up-gap means today's low sits above yesterday's high. Edwards & Magee, Murphy, and ChartSchool split gaps into common/area (inside congestion, usually filled in days), breakaway (leaving a base), runaway/measuring (mid-trend), and exhaustion (end of a move). The first honest disagreement is that those labels are retrospective: ChartSchool's own gap-trading page says the type is only distinguishable after the stock continues up or down, so the taxonomy is a post-hoc description, not a day-0 signal. Edwards & Magee already put the practical test on the day after the gap: continuation makes new highs without filling, exhaustion fails to extend and fills within about a week. The second disagreement is the fill slogan. Murphy calls 'gaps are always filled' a myth. Plastun, Sibande, Gupta and Wohar (North American Journal of Economics and Finance 2020), on DJI/S&P 500/NASDAQ from 1928–2018, find gap-day prices tend to continue in the gap's direction, a temporary momentum effect, and only about 20 percent of those index gaps fill within five days — contrary to the fill myth, with the caveat that this is index overnight structure, not single-name earnings gaps. Bulkowski, on typed individual-stock gaps (~1,100 samples), shows why SEO posts still quote 80 percent fills: area gaps close within a week 85–90 percent of the time (median 3–4 days), exhaustion 60–66 percent (median 5–6 days), continuation 8–1
key_points: Common / breakaway / runaway / exhaustion labels are after-the-fact; Edwards & Magee distinguish continuation from exhaustion on the day after the gap, not on the open.

Murphy, Plastun et al. (index gaps, ~20% fill in 5 days, gap-day continuation), and Bulkowski (breakaway 1% fill in a week vs area 85–90%) all reject 'gaps always fill'; unconditional fills on 3%+ stock gaps match a random walk.
Read gap_analysis.filled AND retained_pct together: ~1.0 is a held open, ~0 or negative is the UNH fade (sold intraday) that the filled flag alone misses.
Do not fade a 2%+ unfilled gap hoping for a fill, and do not skip a 3m-RS leader because an unfilled gap exists — that is the TEAM '31.7% unfilled August gap' costume of 'extended.'
Do not BUY the gap bar; the swing entry is the first pullback that holds the gap-day low or the pre-gap high (the fill line).

A runaway/measuring gap is not a new BUY and is not a full measured-move target (continuation gaps are rare; we already discount measured moves). Holders trail; an island (exhaustion up then breakaway down) is a kill.
A daily close that re-accepts through the pre-gap close is invalidating_structure. Gap_held as a directional classifier scored nothing in the 12-year earnings-reaction test — geometry, not a pillar.
entries.how_to_apply: When gap_analysis lists a ≥2% gap in the last 20 sessions, read filled and retained_pct together before any promote or reject. If retained_pct is ≥ ~0.5, filled is false, and a dated fundamental sits under it (earnings_week, todays_8ks/item 1.01), that is the PEG of KB-3704904010: do not BUY the gap bar; write would_buy_at as the first no_supply_pullback that holds the gap-day low (or the pre-gap high / fill line), promote a 50–70% starter, place stop_loss below that named low AND at least stop_engineering.min_stop_distance_pct (aim 1.5–2× ATR, never past 15%), set target_price at the first overhead supply — never at 'the gap fill' and never from a measuring-gap projection — and require 10% upside and 2:1 from that ATR-floored stop; if that geometry cannot clear, pass. If retained_pct is low or negative (UNH shape) or the gap fills within a few sessions, classify it as faded/common/exhaustion: it is not a PEG, and if you already hold, a daily close that re-accepts through the pre-gap close is invalidating_structure. If the gap is unfilled on a 3m-RS leader with no new catalyst, that is extension, not a skip and not a fade — do not reject it the way TEAM was rejected for a 31.7% unf
